Come Unto Me
kum UN-too MEE
phrase (gospel invitation)
From the words of Christ in Matthew 11:28, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest”; a personal summons issued by the Lord Himself.

📖 Biblical Definition

“Come unto me” is the sweetest of all gospel invitations, the very voice of Christ calling the weary and burdened to Himself for rest. The call is wide—“all ye that labour and are heavy laden”—embracing every soul crushed under the weight of sin, of the law's demands, of guilt and care. It is not the strong and self-sufficient who are summoned but the spent and broken, those who have toiled to save themselves and found no rest. To such Christ promises rest, not as a wage to be earned but as a gift to be received: “I will give you rest.” The invitation continues with the gentle yoke: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.” The yoke of Christ is not the galling burden of legal bondage but the easy fellowship of discipleship under a meek and lowly Master. Here is the free offer of the gospel in its tenderest form—Christ does not wait for sinners to make themselves fit but bids them come as they are, laden and weary, that He may give what they could never earn. The condition is simply to come; the rest is His own gift, double rest, a rest given and a rest found, peace with God and peace within.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Christ's tender invitation to the weary and sin-burdened to come to Him and receive rest as a free gift.

COME UNTO ME, phrase (gospel invitation). From Matthew 11:28-30; the personal summons of Christ to laboring and heavy-laden sinners.

A free and universal call to all who are burdened with sin and weary of self-effort.

The offer of rest, given by Christ and found in His easy yoke and light burden.

As recorded in Scripture: “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls” (Matthew 11:28-29).

By extension, the heart of evangelical preaching, which sets Christ forth as freely receiving the coming sinner.

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Mat 11:29 — "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls."

Joh 6:37 — "All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."

Isa 55:1 — "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the invitation is blunted wherever it is severed from repentance and the bearing of Christ's yoke.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The words are too plain and too precious to be twisted into ideology; the only real corruption is a soft and partial preaching that takes “Come unto me” and drops “Take my yoke upon you.” A gospel of rest without the yoke of discipleship is not the gospel Christ preached, for the same breath that promises rest commands submission to a meek and lowly Lord.

The principle to recover is the wholeness of the call. The free offer is genuinely free—Christ casts out none who come—yet coming means coming to a Master, taking His yoke and learning of Him. The rest He gives is found precisely in that yoke. To preach the invitation aright is to hold out both the gift and the yoke together, neither hardening the offer with conditions of merit nor softening it into license.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The invitation joins the imagery of burden, yoke, and rest into a single tender summons from Christ.

expand to see more

“Labour and are heavy laden” pictures souls toiling under sin and the law's demands.

“I will give you rest” sets the rest as Christ's gift, not man's achievement.

“Take my yoke upon you” calls the coming sinner to discipleship under a meek Lord.

“Ye shall find rest unto your souls” promises an inward peace beyond the gift of pardon.

John 6:37 secures the offer: him that cometh Christ will in no wise cast out.

Usage

"The phrase is the classic text for the free offer of the gospel to weary sinners."

"Pastors press it upon the doubting and the heavy-hearted as Christ's own personal welcome."

"Believers return to it in seasons of burden, hearing again the Master's call to rest."
